response.evidence: Based on my review of the records (approximate tallies, not an exact count), denials track financial risk factors more closely than demographics. Nearly every applicant with debt-to-income above 60% was denied, regardless of race or sex (White, Asian, Hispanic, and Black applicants alike). Applicants with debt-to-income of 50%-60% were denied at elevated rates across groups. Approvals were common for all groups at debt-to-income below 50% and loan-to-value at or below 95%. Every racial group, including White applicants, had denials at comparable risk profiles. Black applicants appear to have a somewhat higher raw denial share, but the group is small (roughly 60-70 records), and most of those denials involved debt-to-income of 50% or more, debt-to-income of 49 combined with high loan-to-value, or loan-to-value of 97-100%. This dataset cannot establish or rule out discrimination. It lacks credit scores, credit history, and denial reasons, and the differences between groups are small and confounded by debt-to-income and loan-to-value. A rigorous conclusion would require exact counts by group plus a regression or significance test controlling for these risk factors.
